facts: Glasgow Cathedral is the only mainland Scottish medieval cathedral to have survived the Reformation largely intact.
It stands on the traditional burial site of St Mungo, the city's patron saint and founder.
High Street station is the nearest stop to both the cathedral and the Glasgow Necropolis.
Kelvingrove holds one of Europe's great civic art collections, including works by Salvador Dali.
The Victorian red sandstone building opened in 1901 for the Glasgow International Exhibition.
Partick station is a major interchange, also connecting to the Glasgow Subway.
The Riverside Museum, designed by Zaha Hadid, tells the story of Glasgow's transport and shipbuilding history.
It sits on the banks of the River Clyde, close to where many famous ships were once built.
The Tall Ship Glenlee, a restored 1896 sailing ship, is moored beside the museum.
Stirling Castle was one of the most important strongholds in Scotland, site of several key sieges.
Mary, Queen of Scots was crowned here as an infant in 1543.
Stirling sits at a strategic crossing point of the River Forth, controlling routes into the Highlands.
The Wallace Monument commemorates William Wallace, victor of the nearby Battle of Stirling Bridge in 1297.
The tower stands 67 metres tall on the summit of Abbey Craig.
It was completed in 1869, funded largely by public subscription.
Dunblane Cathedral dates largely from the 13th century, with a much older Norman tower.
The building fell into ruin after the Reformation before being restored in the 1890s.
Dunblane is the birthplace of tennis champion Andy Murray.
Loch Lomond is the largest loch in Great Britain by surface area.
Balloch sits at the loch's southern tip, within Loch Lomond and the Trossachs National Park.
The loch contains around 30 islands, including the inhabited Inchmurrin.
The 21-arch viaduct, completed in 1901, became internationally famous after featuring in the Harry Potter films.
It also marks the spot where Bonnie Prince Charlie raised his standard in 1745, beginning the Jacobite Rising.
The Jacobite steam train crosses the viaduct on its route between Fort William and Mallaig.
Ben Nevis is the highest mountain in the British Isles, at 1,345 metres.
Fort William, at its foot, is often called the 'Outdoor Capital of the UK'.
The West Highland Line to Fort William is regularly voted one of the world's most scenic rail journeys.
Mallaig is the terminus of the 'Road to the Isles' and a key ferry port to Skye and the Small Isles.
The town developed as a herring fishing port in the late 19th century.
Mallaig station is the western end of the scenic West Highland Line.
McCaig's Tower, an unfinished Colosseum-style folly, overlooks Oban Bay.
Oban is often called the 'Gateway to the Isles', with ferries to Mull, Iona, Islay and Colonsay.
The town is also known for its whisky distillery, one of Scotland's oldest, founded in 1794.
Corrour, at 408 metres above sea level, is the highest mainline railway station in the UK.
It has no road access at all, reached only by rail or on foot across Rannoch Moor.
The station featured in the film Trainspotting, in a scene set on the surrounding moor.
Rannoch Moor is one of the last great wildernesses in Europe, a vast expanse of bog and lochans.
The railway across it was a major engineering challenge, floated on a raft of brushwood and ash.
Rannoch station is one of the most remote in Britain, with very limited road access.

landmark: Falls of Cruachan & Cruachan Power Station
facts: Cruachan Power Station, nicknamed 'the Hollow Mountain', is built entirely inside Ben Cruachan.
It is a pumped-storage hydroelectric station, able to reach full power within seconds.
Falls of Cruachan station is a seasonal request stop, one of the smallest on the network.
Loch Awe is the longest freshwater loch in Scotland, stretching over 40 kilometres.
The ruined Kilchurn Castle sits at its northern end, a popular photography spot.
Loch Awe station serves the small village on the line to Oban.
Bothwell Castle is one of the largest and finest medieval castles in Scotland.
It changed hands repeatedly during the Wars of Scottish Independence.
Uddingston is also known as the birthplace of the Tunnock's teacake, made at a factory in the town.
New Lanark is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, a remarkably preserved cotton mill village founded in 1786.
Reformer Robert Owen ran the mills here, pioneering progressive ideas about workers' welfare.
The village sits on the River Clyde below the town of Lanark.
Culzean Castle, on the Ayrshire coast, was designed by Robert Adam in the late 18th century.
General Eisenhower was given a private apartment in the castle in recognition of his wartime role.
Maybole is the nearest railway station, with the castle reached by road.
Poet Robert Burns was born in Alloway in 1759, in a cottage now preserved as a museum.
The nearby Burns Monument and Brig o' Doon feature in his poem Tam o' Shanter.
Ayr is the main town on the Ayrshire coast, with one of Scotland's finest sandy beaches.
Prestwick has a direct rail link into the airport terminal, unusual for a UK regional airport.
It was the only place in the UK Elvis Presley is officially recorded as having set foot, during a 1960 stopover.
The airport is renowned for having some of the most reliable flying weather in Scotland.
Robert Burns spent his final years in Dumfries and is buried in a mausoleum in St Michael's Churchyard.
Dumfries is nicknamed 'the Queen of the South', also the name of its football club.
The town sits on the River Nith in south-west Scotland.
Gretna Green became famous for runaway weddings after Scots law allowed marriage at a younger age than England's.
Couples were traditionally married over the anvil in the village's Old Blacksmith's Shop.
The village sits just across the border from England, on the West Coast Main Line.
The Battle of Largs in 1263 marked a turning point in Scotland's struggle against Norwegian control of the western isles.
Vikingar!, a heritage attraction in the town, tells the story of the Viking age in Scotland.
Largs is a popular Clyde coast resort, with ferries to the Isle of Cumbrae.
Wemyss Bay station, opened in 1903, is celebrated for its elegant curved glass-roofed concourse.
It connects directly to the ferry for Rothesay on the Isle of Bute.
The station is a Category A listed building, recognised as one of Scotland's finest.
The Cloch Lighthouse, near Gourock, has guided ships on the Firth of Clyde since 1797.
Gourock is a ferry terminal for routes to Dunoon and other Clyde coast towns.
The town's outdoor swimming pool is one of Scotland's few remaining heated seawater lidos.
The Hill House was designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh, a masterpiece of Scottish architecture completed in 1904.
Helensburgh is the birthplace of John Logie Baird, a pioneer of television.
The town sits on the Firth of Clyde, opposite the Rosneath peninsula.
Dumbarton Castle sits on Dumbarton Rock, a volcanic plug overlooking the River Clyde.
It has one of the longest recorded histories of any fortified site in Britain.
Dumbarton was once the capital of the ancient kingdom of Strathclyde.
Paisley Abbey was founded in 1163 and is linked to the origins of the Stewart royal dynasty.
The town gave its name to the paisley pattern, popularised by its 19th-century textile industry.
Paisley Gilmour Street is one of the busiest stations in Scotland outside Glasgow and Edinburgh.
Motherwell was once home to Ravenscraig, at its peak the largest hot strip steel mill in western Europe.
The town's name may derive from a well dedicated to the Virgin Mary.
Motherwell is a key railway junction in North Lanarkshire.
Chatelherault was built as a hunting lodge for the Dukes of Hamilton in the 1730s.
The country park sits in the Avon Gorge, with woodland trails and red deer.
Hamilton was historically the county town of Lanarkshire.
The Falkirk Wheel is the world's only rotating boat lift, connecting the Forth and Clyde and Union canals.
It replaced a flight of 11 locks that had fallen into disuse.
Falkirk Grahamston is the more central of the town's two stations.
Kelburn Castle has been home to the Boyle family, Earls of Glasgow, for over 800 years.
Its grounds feature a giant graffiti-covered mural on the castle walls, painted by Brazilian artists in 2007.
Fairlie is a small village on the Ayrshire coast, with ferries to Cumbrae from nearby Largs.
The Scottish Maritime Museum in Irvine preserves historic vessels linked to the town's shipbuilding past.
Irvine was designated a Scottish new town in 1966.
The town sits at the mouth of the River Irvine on the Ayrshire coast.
Royal Troon has hosted The Open Championship multiple times.
Troon developed as a harbour town before becoming a popular Ayrshire golfing resort.
The town's beach looks out towards the Isle of Arran.
Dean Castle, in Kilmarnock, houses collections of medieval armour and musical instruments.
Kilmarnock published the first edition of Robert Burns' poems in 1786.
The town was historically a centre of the Scotch whisky blending industry, home to Johnnie Walker.

landmark: Girvan's harbour and Ailsa Craig views
facts: Girvan looks out towards Ailsa Craig, a granite island famous for producing curling stones.
The town developed as a herring fishing port in the 18th and 19th centuries.
Girvan sits on the Ayrshire coast on the line towards Stranraer.
Stranraer was historically the main ferry port to Northern Ireland before services moved to nearby Cairnryan.
The town sits on Loch Ryan in south-west Scotland.
Stranraer is the western terminus of the line from Glasgow via Ayr.

landmark: Crianlarich, the crossroads of the Highlands
facts: Crianlarich is where the West Highland Line splits, one branch to Oban and one to Fort William.
The village sits on the West Highland Way long-distance walking route.
Crianlarich is surrounded by Munros, Scottish mountains over 3,000 feet.

landmark: Ardlui & the head of Loch Lomond
facts: Ardlui sits at the northern tip of Loch Lomond, where the loch narrows into the surrounding mountains.
A small passenger ferry links Ardlui station to the settlement of Ardlui itself.
The village marks the transition from the loch's broad southern waters to its narrow highland reaches.

landmark: Tyndrum, Scotland's smallest place with two stations
facts: Tyndrum is unusual in having two railway stations, Upper and Lower, serving the Fort William and Oban lines.
The village was once a centre of lead and later gold prospecting.
Tyndrum sits at a key junction on the West Highland Way.

landmark: Bridge of Orchy's remote mountain scenery
facts: Bridge of Orchy sits at the foot of Beinn Dorain, a distinctive conical mountain.
The station is a popular starting point for walkers on the West Highland Way.
It marks the transition from Highland glens into the wilds of Rannoch Moor.

landmark: Bridge of Allan's Victorian spa heritage
facts: Bridge of Allan developed as a fashionable spa town after mineral springs were promoted in the 1820s.
The village sits at the foot of the Ochil Hills, close to Stirling.
Its well-preserved Victorian architecture reflects its resort-era prosperity.
Cumbernauld was designated a Scottish new town in 1955, known for its distinctive Brutalist town centre.
The town has been both praised and criticised internationally for its ambitious 1960s urban design.
Cumbernauld sits roughly midway between Glasgow and Stirling.
Kilwinning Abbey is linked to the founding traditions of Scottish Freemasonry.
The town's name derives from St Winnin, an early Christian missionary.
Kilwinning is a key junction on the Ayrshire coast line.
Auchinleck was the ancestral home of James Boswell, biographer of Samuel Johnson.
The village was historically a mining community in the Ayrshire coalfield.
Auchinleck sits on the line towards Kilmarnock and Glasgow.
Airdrie grew rapidly during the Industrial Revolution around coal, iron and weaving.
The Airdrie to Bathgate rail link reopened in 2010 after decades of closure.
The town sits in North Lanarkshire, close to Coatbridge.
Gartmorn Dam, near Alloa, is one of the oldest reservoirs in Scotland, built in the early 18th century.
Alloa was historically a centre of brewing and glassmaking on the Firth of Forth.
Alloa's rail line reopened to passengers in 2008 after a long closure.
The remains of a Roman bath house and latrine, built around 140 AD, survive in the middle of Bearsden.
It was part of a fort on the Antonine Wall, the northernmost frontier of the Roman Empire.
Bearsden is now a residential suburb on the northwestern edge of Glasgow.
Sanquhar Post Office is recognised by Guinness World Records as the oldest continuously operating post office in the world, dating to 1712.
Sanquhar also has one of the oldest surviving royal burgh charters in Scotland, granted in 1598.
The town sits in Upper Nithsdale, on the line between Kilmarnock and Dumfries.
Neilston was once a centre of cotton and thread manufacturing in the Levern Valley.
The village sits at the southern end of the Glasgow suburban rail network.
Nearby Neilston Pad hill offers panoramic views back towards Glasgow.
